analysis.one_liner: Taxes employers that cut prescription drug coverage for retirees already over 65.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House Ways and Means subcommittee on February 14, 2005, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: When employers drop prescription drug coverage for retirees who are already 65, this bill would charge them a tax of $750 per single-coverage retiree and $1,500 per retiree with family or other coverage. The money raised would go into Medicare's prescription drug account. The goal is to make it expensive for companies to cut drug benefits for people who already retired and were promised them.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees age 65 and older who earned prescription drug coverage during their working years and would otherwise lose it when an employer cuts retiree benefits. The tax gives employers a reason to keep the coverage in place, and any tax paid by employers who cut coverage anyway flows into Medicare's prescription drug account.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees over 65 with employer drug coverage

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax on employers or employee organizations that terminate prescription drug benefits for a retiree who was 65 or older at the time of termination and left the employer before the bill's enactment.
Sets the tax at $750 per retiree with self-only drug coverage and $1,500 per retiree with any other coverage level.
Requires the Treasury to transfer the tax revenue to the Medicare Prescription Drug Account in the federal Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that terminate retiree prescription drug coverage, at $750 to $1,500 per affected retiree. Employers that keep the coverage pay nothing. The tax applies only to terminations taking effect after enactment.

drawbacks.text: The tax raises the cost of terminating retiree drug coverage, which could make employers more hesitant to offer retiree health benefits in the first place, since the obligation attaches to anyone who retired before enactment.

It only protects retirees who were already 65 and already separated from the employer, so it does nothing for future retirees, and it does not restore coverage for people whose benefits were already cut before enactment.
Revenue is modest: at $750 to $1,500 per affected retiree, the money transferred to Medicare is small relative to the drug costs those retirees may face without employer coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it covers — retirees already over 65 with promised drug benefits — the bill is a straightforward protection: it makes cutting their coverage expensive, and any employer that cuts it anyway pays into Medicare's drug account. The costs are real but narrow: a per-retiree charge on employers that drop benefits, and a possible chilling effect on future retiree benefit offers, though the bill deliberately excludes future retirees from its reach. On balance the design is targeted and the downside limited, but the bill never advanced far enough to be tested in committee or amended.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in a House Ways and Means subcommittee from two weeks after introduction until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Eliot Engel introduced the bill in the House on February 1, 2005.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the day it was introduced.
On February 14, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where no further action was recorded for the rest of the 109th Congress.
No member of the House cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that have dropped or want to drop retiree drug coverage face no penalty, and the retirees the bill aimed to protect got no new protection.

for.name: Rep. Eliot Engel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 1, 2005; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health
against.role: Subcommittee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 14, 2005 and took no recorded action for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill at full committee for two weeks before referring it to the Health Subcommittee, and never scheduled a markup or floor action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors from either party, and died in a Republican-run committee without a recorded vote, so no party split was ever measured.

industries.industry: Large employers and unions providing retiree health coverage
industries.note: The bill taxes them $750 to $1,500 each time they terminate prescription drug coverage for a retiree over 65, making it costlier to shift promised retiree drug costs off their books. Their interest in dropping the coverage runs directly against the retirees who were promised it.

When employers cut retiree drug coverage, retirees generally move onto Medicare drug coverage delivered by private plans, gaining those plans new customers. By making terminations expensive, the bill reduces that flow of new enrollees.
